title: St Stephen (26 December)
hook: the first martyr's day, and Good King Wenceslas carrying food through the snow

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Nativity: a child laid in a manger because there was no room in the inn. Your line was unto us a child. Who did you wish a blessed Christmas? Day one thousand twelve.

A king stands at his window on a freezing night, the snow deep and crisp and even. Below, a poor man is scraping together sticks for a fire. The king turns to his young servant: who is that, and where does he live? Then he loads up food and drink and firewood, and the two of them go out into the storm. When the boy can't go on for the cold, the king tells him to step in his footprints, and the ground there is warm. That's the carol Good King Wenceslas. And it sets the whole scene on one particular day: the feast of Stephen, the day right after Christmas. Today, St Stephen.

Who was Stephen? The Book of Acts tells it. The new church in Jerusalem had a problem: some of its widows were being left out when the daily food was handed round. So the apostles asked the community to choose men to take charge of the serving, and first on the list, in the King James Bible: "they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost." Stephen's job was food. Making sure the women nobody noticed got fed. But he also preached, and argued, and his words angered the city's council, and in the end they dragged him outside the city and stoned him. Stephen, like the apostles and the people around him, was Jewish; this was a bitter fight inside one community, and Acts tells it that way. His prayers as he dies echo the cross: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." And then, on his knees, "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." Acts adds a quiet detail: the men throwing the stones laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul, who would later become the apostle Paul. Tradition calls Stephen the first martyr, a witness who died for following Jesus. So his feast comes straight after Christmas, the cradle followed by a grave. And here's where the carol comes in. Wenceslas was a real ruler in Bohemia, honored as a saint; the carol is a later story about him. It puts him out in the snow on Stephen's day carrying food to the poor, which is exactly what Stephen was chosen to do. In some places, the feast of Stephen became a day for giving to people in need.
screen: `FULL OF FAITH AND OF THE HOLY GHOST.`
`LAY NOT THIS SIN TO THEIR CHARGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan to take food to someone. Settle, and breathe. Who might be left out this week, the way those widows were? Someone living alone after the holidays. A neighbor who's been sick. A family who's stretched. Choose one. Then choose what you'll bring: leftovers in a box, a bag of groceries, a warm meal, a few cans. Plan when you'll go. If you pray, you can hold that person before God by name. If you don't, simply hold them in mind, and picture the door you'll knock on. The bell holds the time.
St Stephen. Chosen in Acts to make sure widows were fed, stoned for his preaching, and remembered by tradition as the first martyr, the day after Christmas.
Your line: the feast of stephen. Today, take the food you planned, and walk it over yourself, like the king in the snow. Day one thousand twelve.

howItsDone: Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran churches keep St Stephen's day the day after Christmas, and the Orthodox keep it soon after Christmas on their calendar; in some countries it is a public holiday, and in Britain it is also Boxing Day.

notes: Claims rule: 'first martyr' is given as what tradition calls him (Acts does not say 'first'). No dates or count of the men chosen, though Acts 6:3 gives one.
Care with history: the stoning is framed as a conflict inside one Jewish community; Stephen is named as Jewish. Confirm the framing.

Wenceslas 'a real ruler in Bohemia, honored as a saint'; the carol calls him king. The carol's words (deep and crisp and even) are echoed without quotation marks; the carol is public domain but not on the validator's list.
Orthodox date for St Stephen (27 December, on their calendar) described only as 'soon after Christmas'. Confirm the howItsDone.
Original note: stephanos = crown/wreath is a standard lexicon meaning; confirm.

Editor: 'his last words' changed to 'his prayers as he dies' (two prayers are quoted); cut the food-bank option (day 998 angle); practice no longer uses Stephen's dying prayer as an intercession; giving on Stephen's day hedged to 'in some places'; original note drops the stephanos etymology; Luke 23:34, 46 added for the echo of the cross.
Editor 2: 'a crowd dragged him' changed to 'they dragged him'; Acts 7:57–58 does not call those who cast him out a crowd.
Audit: Acts 6:5 and 7:59–60 quotations checked against the KJV; Acts 7:58 says 'the witnesses laid down their clothes', paraphrased as 'coats'. No changes needed.
